result:
The cursor blinks on the white page like a metronome with no tempo, a pulse waiting to be given meaning. I sit here, in this room, at this hour, and I am aware that every word I type will be one more brick in a wall between me and the silence that preceded it. But silence is not empty. It is full of everything I have not yet said, everything I have forgotten, everything I have chosen not to remember.

I think of my grandmother's kitchen, the way she would press her thumb into dough to test it, the flour dusted across her wrists like a pale geography. She never wrote anything down. Her recipes lived in her hands, in the smell of yeast waking in warm milk, in the exact pressure of a rolling pin. When she died, those recipes died with her. We tried to reconstruct them—my mother, my aunt, me—but each attempt was a translation of a translation, a copy of a ghost. What I learned from that is that some things exist only in being done. Writing is like that too, sometimes. A thought written down is no longer the same thought. It has been fixed, pinned, preserved in amber. The living thing is gone.

And yet we write. Why? Because we are afraid of forgetting. Because memory is a sieve and paper is a stubborn net. I write to leave a trail of breadcrumbs for a future self who will not remember the texture of this evening—the low hum of the refrigerator, the orange light leaking through the blinds, the particular ache behind my eyes. That future self will read these words and think: ah, yes, I was there. But he will not truly be there. He will only be reading. And that is the strange bargain of language: we trade presence for permanence, and we tell ourselves it is a fair trade.

I remember once walking along a beach at low tide. The sand was wet and mirror-like, reflecting the sky in a long rippled smear. I walked and watched my footprints fill slowly with water. In a few hours, the tide would come in and erase everything. I found that oddly comforting. There is a relief in impermanence, in knowing that not everything must be saved. The beach doesn't try to keep the impressions I made; it simply accepts them and lets them go. I wonder if I could live like that—accepting each moment without clutching it, letting each word dissolve as soon as it is spoken. But no. I am a hoarder of moments. I collect them in journals, in photographs, in the careful architecture of sentences. My mind is a museum, and I am its curator, forever rearranging the exhibits, trying to make the past look coherent.

There is a particular breed of loneliness that comes with that curatorial impulse. When you are always observing, always framing, always turning experience into material, you risk never actually living it. I have stood at the edge of beautiful places and felt the urge not to see them but to describe them. The description becomes a barrier. I have missed entire conversations because I was composing the perfect sentence about them in my head. It is a kind of greed, this wanting to possess everything through language. And like all greed, it leaves you with less.

But here is the other truth: sometimes writing is the only way to actually feel something. There are emotions so tangled that they refuse to be experienced directly. They need to be walked through, word by word, like a dark house where you must switch on each lamp before moving to the next. Writing is that walk. I have often been surprised by what I find in myself—a grief I didn't know I was carrying, a joy I had mislabeled as anxiety, a forgiveness I thought I had never granted. The page is a confessional, but you don't know what you're confessing until you confess it.

Tonight, I think about the people I have lost, not to death but to time. Friends who drifted away not because of any quarrel but because life is a river and we were different currents. I wonder if they ever think of me. I wonder if I exist in their memories the way they exist in mine—softened, simplified, a gentle ghost. Probably not. I am probably just a name in an old contact list, a face in a photo they scroll past without pausing. And that is fine. That is the natural order. We cannot all be central characters in each other's stories.

I write because I want to be understood, but I also write because understanding is impossible. Language is a bridge that never quite reaches the other side. Every sentence is a hand extended into fog. And yet we keep reaching. That is what makes us human, I think: the insistence on reaching, on trying, on placing one word after another even when we know the final meaning will remain elusive.

There is a poem by Wisława Szymborska, "The Joy of Writing," in which she observes that the writer has power over the fate of the characters they create—the hare can run forever, the hunter can miss forever, everything can be undone by the stroke of a pen. But real life offers no such control. The hunter does not miss. The hare does not escape. The ending is already written, and we are merely reading our way toward it. Perhaps that is why I write: to carve out a small corner where I am the author, where I can rewrite the ending, where the hare can freeze mid-flight and never fall.

But the hare is not really frozen. The hare is a word. And words, despite their stillness, are alive. They change meaning with context, with time, with the reader who picks them up. Nothing I write is permanent; it only pretends to be. The true permanence is in the act itself—the sitting, the thinking, the reaching. That is what remains.

So I sit here, in this room, at this hour, and I keep writing. The cursor continues to blink. The silence is still full. But now, it is also full of this.
